paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent facing a sequence of related problems can potentially reuse more than solutions to individual tasks. It can also reuse experience about how to explore. This paper studies how knowledge gained earlier in an agent’s lifetime can help it gather useful information when a new problem arrives.

The central move is to treat the search for an exploration strategy as another reinforcement learning problem. The original problems are Markov decision processes, and the proposed framework places the choice of how to explore at a higher level. This makes exploration itself something the agent can optimize through experience across related problems.

The authors demonstrate that an exploration strategy learned this way can exploit recurring structure among tasks. Their experiments show benefits from optimizing exploration within the proposed framework. The contribution is therefore a way to transfer experience about learning behavior: earlier tasks can inform how the agent investigates a new task, helping it use similarities between problems while seeking a solution.
neurips-2019-a-meta-mdp-approach-to-expl.tldr: The paper formulates learning how to explore related reinforcement learning tasks as a reinforcement learning problem itself.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can represent complex relationships, but their behavior depends on graph structure and repeated nonlinear transformations. This paper studies that behavior through two familiar image operations: filtering and propagation. Its goal is to connect mathematical properties of a graph network to the way information moves through an image.

The authors recursively define an adaptive graph neural network and express it as a label propagation system. Three ingredients organize the analysis: a guiding map, a graph Laplacian, and node weights. The guiding map and weights determine whether the network produces filtering or propagation diffusion, while the Laplacian kernel controls the diffusion pattern. These relationships give specific network components interpretable roles.

The practical application is quotient image analysis, which recovers reflectance ratios for analyzing or adjusting images. The authors introduce a regularization structure with guided features and build the QIA-GNN framework around it. Experiments demonstrate applications including face illumination synthesis and low-light enhancement. The work connects an explanation of graph-network behavior with a framework for solving image editing problems.
neurips-2019-adaptive-gnn-for-image-anal.tldr: An adaptive graph neural network connects filtering and propagation theory to practical image analysis and editing.

paragraphs: Training a classifier to withstand adversarial perturbations can require substantially more data than ordinary classification. That creates a practical obstacle when obtaining labels is expensive. This paper asks whether unlabeled examples can supply much of the additional information needed for robust learning, reducing reliance on a larger labeled dataset.

The authors support this idea theoretically and experimentally. In a simple statistical setting, they show that learning an adversarially robust model from unlabeled data has sample complexity matching the fully supervised case up to constant factors. This is a result for that setting, establishing that labels need not account for the entire data requirement for robustness.

Their Unsupervised Adversarial Training approach improves robust accuracy by a reported 21.7% over training with 4,000 supervised examples alone on CIFAR-10. It captures more than 95% of the improvement obtained from an equal number of labeled additions. Using extra, uncurated images also yields a reported 4% improvement over the previous state of the art against the strongest known attack. These findings show that unlabeled data can be useful even without careful curation.
neurips-2019-are-labels-required-for-imp.tldr: Unlabeled data can deliver much of the adversarial robustness improvement otherwise obtained from additional labeled examples.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents often face competing requirements, such as completing a task while limiting time or energy use. Combining all requirements into one reward makes their balance difficult to specify. Constrained reinforcement learning offers another formulation: optimize an objective while explicitly imposing requirements on other aspects of behavior.

A difficulty is that the resulting optimization problem is nonconvex, so primal-dual methods do not automatically come with guarantees of finding an optimum. This paper establishes that the constrained reinforcement learning problem it studies has zero duality gap. In other words, its optimal value agrees with that of a corresponding dual problem, which is convex.

That equality supplies theoretical support for solving the problem through the dual formulation. The authors also show that the result substantially carries over when policies have a good parametrization, including neural networks, and connect their analysis to existing primal-dual algorithms to establish convergence to an optimal solution. The parametrization qualification matters: the abstract ties this extension to how well the chosen policy representation can express the required behavior.
neurips-2019-constrained-reinforcement-l.tldr: The paper establishes zero duality gap for constrained reinforcement learning and provides theoretical support for primal-dual solution methods.

paragraphs: Language model pretraining had shown strong results for English language understanding. This paper extends that approach across languages, investigating whether pretraining can support both cross-lingual classification and machine translation. The aim is to learn language models whose usefulness spans multiple languages and different kinds of downstream tasks.

The authors propose two ways to train cross-lingual language models. The unsupervised method uses only monolingual text, so it does not depend on paired translations. The supervised method uses parallel data through a new cross-lingual language modeling objective. These alternatives address settings with different forms of available language data.

The reported results improve the state of the art in cross-lingual classification and both unsupervised and supervised translation. On XNLI, the accuracy gain is 4.9 absolute percentage points. Unsupervised German-English translation reaches 34.3 BLEU, more than nine points above the previous best, while supervised Romanian-English translation reaches 38.5 BLEU, improving by more than four points. Together, these findings demonstrate the effectiveness of cross-lingual pretraining across the evaluated tasks and data settings.
neurips-2019-cross-lingual-language-mode.tldr: Cross-lingual language model pretraining improves classification and translation using either monolingual text or parallel language data.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing combines imperfect labels from multiple annotators to obtain more reliable labels. The Dawid-Skene model is a classical framework for this task, but understanding when its underlying model can be identified remains important. Existing tensor approaches offer identification guarantees while relying on statistics involving three annotators, which can be difficult to estimate reliably with limited data.

This paper instead builds a framework around pairwise co-occurrences: how responses from pairs of annotators appear together. The authors show that these simpler statistics can identify the Dawid-Skene model under realistic conditions. The approach naturally has lower sample complexity, addressing the data demands that make third-order statistics a practical obstacle.

The paper also develops an efficient algebraic identification algorithm related to structured matrix factorization and convex geometry. A second algorithm strengthens identifiability for more challenging scenarios. Experiments show improvements over existing methods across a variety of settings. The central finding is that pairwise information can support model identification under the stated conditions, enabling algorithms that demand less statistical information from the available annotations.
neurips-2019-crowdsourcing-via-pairwise-.tldr: Pairwise annotator response statistics can identify the Dawid-Skene crowdsourcing model under realistic conditions with lower sample demands.

paragraphs: A voting system must decide both what information to request from voters and how to combine their answers. This paper treats both choices as parts of the design problem. Voters begin with cardinal preferences, which describe the strength of their preferences, and an elicitation rule translates that information into votes.

The aggregation rule then converts those votes into a collective decision. Asking for richer information can require more communication, measured here as the number of bits voters provide. The quality of the collective outcome is measured through distortion: how closely its total social welfare approximates the highest achievable welfare in the worst case.

The authors characterize the Pareto frontier between communication and distortion. This identifies the best tradeoffs between the amount of preference information collected and the resulting worst-case welfare guarantee. The contribution makes explicit that voting efficiency depends on both the reporting format and the decision rule. Designing them together allows the analysis to address how much communication is needed for a particular level of collective decision quality.
neurips-2019-efficient-and-thrifty-votin.tldr: The paper characterizes the best tradeoffs between voter communication and worst-case social welfare when designing both reporting and aggregation rules.

paragraphs: Arbitrary style transfer combines the recognizable structure of a content image with patterns from a style image. This paper addresses challenging cases where existing methods produce too little stylization. The authors suggest that generating the output in a single pass makes it difficult to satisfy both structural and stylistic constraints. This is their proposed explanation for the problem.

ETNet approaches stylization as a sequence of corrections. The model predicts what is wrong with the current result and refines it repeatedly. During each refinement, it processes features representing errors across spatial locations and scales, then converts those processed features into a residual image: an image that supplies a correction to the current output. This gives the model repeated opportunities to improve the stylization.

The authors report improvements over the methods they compare against, including better preservation of semantic structure and style details that adapt more effectively. Their qualitative and quantitative experiments support the value of both progressive refinement and error correction. The findings suggest that explicitly identifying and correcting stylization errors can help reconcile content structure with the desired style patterns.
neurips-2019-etnet-error-transition-netw.tldr: ETNet repeatedly predicts and corrects stylization errors, with reported improvements in content structure and adaptive style details.

paragraphs: Some machine learning applications begin with almost no training data, and collecting each individual measurement has a cost. Icebreaker addresses this starting situation by deciding which feature elements to acquire. The unit of acquisition is an individual data entry, making the framework relevant when measurements can be obtained separately.

The framework introduces a fully Bayesian deep latent Gaussian model called BELGAM. Its inference method combines amortized inference with stochastic gradient Markov chain Monte Carlo to support fast, accurate posterior inference. The model’s quantification of uncertainty then informs two acquisition functions, aimed at filling in missing values and acquiring information for active prediction.

Experiments on machine learning benchmarks, recommender systems, and healthcare applications show that BELGAM performs significantly better than earlier variational autoencoder models when datasets are small. Icebreaker also improves over the evaluated baselines and can achieve better test performance with less training data. The findings connect uncertainty estimation to data collection: a model can use uncertainty to guide which costly measurements are acquired as training begins.
neurips-2019-icebreaker-element-wise-eff.tldr: Icebreaker uses Bayesian uncertainty to select individual data measurements when training begins with little or no data.

paragraphs: Gradient descent can favor particular solutions even when the training objective contains no explicit preference for them. This behavior is called implicit regularization. The paper investigates it in deep matrix factorization, where a sequence of linear transformations represents a matrix, focusing on matrix completion and sensing problems.

The first finding is that increasing depth strengthens a tendency toward low-rank solutions. A low-rank matrix has a more compact underlying structure, so favoring such solutions can help recover the matrix from incomplete information. Theory and experiments support this depth-dependent tendency, and the authors report that it often produces more accurate recovery.

The second finding concerns how to describe that preference mathematically. The authors present theoretical and empirical arguments against the view that simple matrix norms fully capture implicit regularization in this setting. Their results suggest that standard regularizers may be too limited to describe all the effects of gradient-based optimization. The conclusion is a qualified challenge to a common explanatory framework, alongside evidence that depth changes the kinds of solutions optimization favors.
neurips-2019-implicit-regularization-in-.tldr: Deeper matrix factorizations strengthen gradient descent’s bias toward low rank, while simple norms may not fully explain that bias.

paragraphs: Revenue-maximizing auctions traditionally rely on knowing a prior distribution describing bidder demand. Learning that distribution from observed behavior offers an alternative, but repeated participation creates a complication. A bidder may deliberately behave differently early on to influence what the seller learns and obtain more favorable prices later.

The paper calls this strategic overfitting. The issue is that the observations used for learning can themselves be shaped by participants who anticipate the learning process. Consequently, a method that estimates demand well from ordinary samples can still face distorted data and reduced revenue when deployed over repeated auction rounds.

The authors combine differential privacy, mechanism design, and sample complexity tools to construct a repeated auction with three stated properties. It learns demand from past data, achieves approximately optimal revenue, and gives bidders incentives to report truthfully. These properties address learning and strategic behavior together. The contribution is an auction-learning approach whose revenue objective accounts for participants’ ability to influence future decisions through their earlier actions.
neurips-2019-learning-auctions-with-robu.tldr: The paper designs a repeated auction that learns demand, achieves approximately optimal revenue, and incentivizes truthful bidder behavior.

paragraphs: High-dimensional time series can conceal simpler patterns in how states evolve. This paper studies Markov trajectories under the assumption that their transition kernel has low intrinsic rank. That assumption motivates seeking a compact representation that retains information about the process’s dynamics despite the large size of each observed state.

The authors propose an efficient embedding method inspired by diffusion maps. It also leads to a kernel reshaping procedure for improving nonparametric estimation of the transition function. The learned representation can group states into metastable sets, exposing slow dynamics. The paper proves statistical error bounds and bounds on the clustering misclassification rate.

A simulated dynamical system demonstrates recovery of metastable structure. A second experiment uses time series from layers of a Deep-Q-Network playing an Atari game. There, the embedding treats states as similar when they share similar future events, even when their raw observations differ substantially. This illustrates the representation’s purpose: organizing states around their evolution can reveal relationships that their immediate observed appearance does not make obvious.
neurips-2019-learning-low-dimensional-st.tldr: Under a low-rank transition assumption, the method learns compact state representations that capture dynamics and reveal metastable clusters.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification asks a model to recognize classes from very few labeled examples, sometimes only one per class. Unlabeled examples offer additional information, but using the model’s own predictions as labels requires deciding which predictions deserve influence. This paper proposes learning that decision through experience across many few-shot tasks.

The learning-to-self-train method trains on a large collection of semi-supervised tasks. Within each task, a few-shot classifier assigns provisional labels to unlabeled examples. It then repeatedly trains using the original labels together with these pseudo labels, with fine-tuning after each self-training step. The broader training process learns how to select and label useful unlabeled data.

A soft weighting network additionally learns how strongly each pseudo label should contribute to optimization, allowing better pseudo labels to carry more weight. Evaluation on two ImageNet benchmarks shows large improvements over the previous state of the art. The result supports learning the self-training procedure itself: experience across tasks can guide how a classifier expands its limited labeled evidence with predictions on unlabeled examples.
neurips-2019-learning-to-self-train-for-.tldr: Learning to self-train uses meta-learning to select, label, and weight unlabeled examples for few-shot classification.

paragraphs: This paper compares different ways to train two-layer neural networks with quadratic activations. It studies two controlled learning settings: predicting an unknown quadratic function from Gaussian inputs, and identifying which of two centered Gaussian components produced an input. These settings make it possible to analyze differences between training regimes mathematically.

The random-features regime trains only the second-layer weights. The neural-tangent regime trains a linear approximation of the network around its initial parameters. Full training adjusts every weight. The comparison therefore examines how restricting the changes a network can make affects its prediction risk, even for relatively simple target problems.

For quadratic-function prediction, the authors prove that the gap between these regimes can be potentially unbounded when the number of neurons is below the input dimension. When the neuron count exceeds the dimension, the problem becomes substantially easier, and both neural-tangent and fully trained learning attain zero risk. These findings show that the adequacy of restricted training depends strongly on network width relative to dimensionality in the studied setting.
neurips-2019-limitations-of-lazy-trainin.tldr: For the studied quadratic networks, restricted training can have a potentially unbounded risk gap when network width is below input dimension.

paragraphs: Distributed training can spend substantial time communicating between workers. Local stochastic gradient descent reduces these exchanges by letting each worker update its model on local data and averaging models periodically. This paper strengthens the theoretical understanding of how infrequent that communication can be while retaining the benefits of multiple workers.

For losses satisfying the Polyak-Kojasiewicz condition, the authors show that O((pT)^(1/3)) communication rounds suffice for an error of O(1/(pT)). Here, p is the number of workers and T is the number of updates per worker. The dependence on p represents linear speedup. Earlier theory required more communication and restricted comparable guarantees to strongly convex losses.

The paper also introduces an adaptive synchronization scheme and gives a general condition under which it achieves linear speedup. Experiments on AWS EC2 and an internal GPU cluster validate the theory. The findings indicate that local SGD can retain its convergence benefits with substantially fewer synchronization rounds than previous analyses suggested, under the loss conditions and synchronization requirements established in the paper.
neurips-2019-local-sgd-with-periodic-ave.tldr: A tighter analysis shows that local SGD can achieve linear speedup with fewer communication rounds under the Polyak-Kojasiewicz condition.

paragraphs: Adversarial attacks can change a network’s classification by altering its input. This paper examines what happens inside the network during a PGD attack. Its empirical analysis finds that the attacked example’s internal representation moves closer to an incorrect class, connecting classification failures to the geometry of learned representations.

Motivated by that observation, the authors use metric learning to regularize the representation space under attack. Metric learning concerns the relationships and distances between representations, so it provides a way to influence the structure implicated by their analysis. The method carefully samples examples for this learning process to produce more robust classifiers.

The learned representations also support detection of previously unseen adversarial examples. Quantitative experiments report robustness accuracy improvements of up to 4% and detection improvements of up to 6% by an area-under-the-curve measure over prior work. These are the reported maximum gains across the evaluations. The findings support representation geometry as a useful target for improving both resistance to adversarial inputs and the ability to identify them.
neurips-2019-metric-learning-for-adversa.tldr: Metric learning improves adversarial robustness and detection by regularizing the internal representations that attacks shift toward incorrect classes.

paragraphs: Dynamic functional connectivity describes how the covariance between neurological signals changes over time. Such changes are believed to matter for cognition, but establishing their presence and character is difficult. Neuroimaging data contain many variables and substantial noise, making a reliable description of changing relationships a demanding statistical problem.

This paper introduces a latent factor Gaussian process model to learn a compact representation of those connectivity dynamics. The latent-factor formulation provides a parsimonious account of the evolving relationships. The resulting model supports both inference and visualization, allowing the estimated time-varying connectivity to be examined as part of the analysis.

The authors illustrate its scientific use with rat local field potential recordings collected during a complex non-spatial memory task. Applying the model provides evidence of stimulus differentiation. This result demonstrates how the representation can help investigate task-related patterns in neural activity. The contribution combines a statistical model for noisy, high-dimensional connectivity with an example of how its inferred dynamics can inform interpretation of a neuroscience experiment.
neurips-2019-modeling-dynamic-functional.tldr: A latent factor Gaussian process models changing neural connectivity compactly and reveals evidence of stimulus differentiation in rat recordings.

paragraphs: Even carefully designed or automatically searched neural networks can contain redundant operations. These operations consume memory and computation and may also hurt predictive performance. This paper studies how to improve an existing architecture’s operations while respecting a constraint against additional computation, a problem the authors describe as NP-hard.

To make the task manageable, they formulate architecture modification as a Markov decision process. A Neural Architecture Transformer, or NAT, learns modification policies through reinforcement learning. Its changes replace redundant operations with more computationally efficient alternatives, such as skip connections, or remove connections. The learned policy therefore acts on an existing architecture to improve its design.

The authors apply NAT to both manually constructed networks and architectures produced by neural architecture search. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet show that the transformed architectures significantly outperform their original versions and architectures optimized by existing methods. These findings indicate that architecture search or manual design can leave useful opportunities for subsequent optimization, and that a learned transformation policy can exploit those opportunities in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2019-nat-neural-architecture-tra.tldr: NAT uses reinforcement learning to replace redundant network operations with efficient alternatives and improve existing architectures.

paragraphs: The effectiveness of a gradient method depends on the geometry of both the allowed solutions and the gradients it encounters. This paper studies those dependencies for online and stochastic convex optimization. It asks when stochastic and adaptive gradient methods achieve minimax optimality, meaning the best possible worst-case performance for the setting.

The authors show that diagonal preconditioning of stochastic gradient methods is minimax optimal when the constraint set is quadratically convex. Diagonal preconditioning adjusts the scaling of individual coordinates. The result therefore identifies a geometric condition under which this form of coordinate scaling is sufficient to attain the optimal worst-case guarantee.

The paper also establishes a converse: when constraints are not quadratically convex, these methods can be far from optimal. Balls defined by an l_p norm with p below two are a stated example. Together, the positive and negative results support concrete guidance about choosing adaptive, mirror, or stochastic gradient methods. The contribution ties method selection to the structure of the optimization problem through a characterization of where particular guarantees hold.
neurips-2019-necessary-and-sufficient-ge.tldr: The paper characterizes constraint geometries where diagonally preconditioned stochastic gradient methods are minimax optimal or far from optimal.

paragraphs: When comparisons are noisy, identifying the preferred item once does not reliably establish an ordering. This paper studies how to recover the complete, exact ranking with a specified confidence while making as few comparisons as possible. The comparison choices can adapt as evidence accumulates, allowing the procedure to respond to what earlier outcomes reveal.

The analysis covers instances with unequal noise levels and avoids restriction to a particular comparison model. It also targets exact ranking without advance knowledge of the instance. These features matter because comparison difficulty can vary across items, and algorithms cannot always rely on knowing that difficulty before they begin gathering evidence.

The authors first establish lower bounds on the number of pairwise comparisons required, then develop pairwise algorithms that are optimal or nearly optimal relative to those bounds. They extend the analysis to comparisons involving multiple items at once. Numerical results show improvements over the state of the art. The combined bounds describe both achievable comparison efficiency and fundamental obstacles to recovering an exact ordering from noisy observations.
neurips-2019-on-sample-complexity-upper-.tldr: The paper gives lower bounds and nearly optimal algorithms for exact ranking from noisy comparisons without prior instance knowledge.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks require substantial computation, storage, and memory bandwidth, including for intermediate values. Quantization reduces the numerical precision used to represent these values, but recovering the resulting accuracy loss often requires access to the full training dataset and further training. Those requirements complicate deployment of an already trained model.

This paper introduces a practical approach to four-bit post-training quantization for both weights and activations. It requires neither fine-tuning of the quantized network nor the complete dataset. The authors propose three complementary techniques that minimize quantization error at the tensor level. Two of these techniques have closed-form analytical solutions.

Combining the methods produces accuracy only a few percent below the state-of-the-art baseline across a broad range of convolutional models, according to the reported results. The contribution is a deployment-oriented tradeoff: substantially reduced numerical precision with a relatively small reported accuracy loss, achieved without another training stage. Targeting both stored weights and intermediate activations addresses two sources of the memory demands described in the paper.
neurips-2019-post-training-4-bit-quantiz.tldr: Three complementary techniques enable four-bit quantization of network weights and activations without fine-tuning or access to the full dataset.

paragraphs: Optical sensors bring researchers closer to observing voltage throughout a neuron’s dendritic tree, but noisy measurements and limited sampling rates complicate interpretation. Statistical methods must therefore denoise and interpolate the signals to recover voltage dynamics from a single trial. Earlier approaches used limited linear models or struggled to scale to large trees.

The authors introduce a fully Bayesian nonlinear generative model with relatively few parameters for each cell compartment. It accommodates different dynamics across compartments and incorporates biophysical knowledge to constrain behavior both within and between them. This combines a flexible account of voltage evolution with structure supplied by the biology.

An augmented Gibbs sampling algorithm estimates a full posterior distribution over voltage across space and time. The output therefore includes uncertainty about the reconstructed dynamics. The nonlinear smoother outperforms previous linear methods and handles much larger systems than earlier sequential Monte Carlo approaches. The findings address both modeling capacity and computational scale, making richer statistical reconstruction feasible for larger dendritic systems.
neurips-2019-scalable-bayesian-inference.tldr: A nonlinear Bayesian model reconstructs dendritic voltage with uncertainty while scaling to larger systems than previous sampling approaches.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning aims to reuse experience gathered by earlier policies. This paper considers the demanding case where that dataset is fixed and the agent cannot collect additional experience. In this setting, learning must work with the available action coverage, making sensitivity to the data distribution especially consequential.

The authors identify bootstrapping error as a major source of instability. Value updates can rely on actions outside the training distribution, and errors associated with those actions accumulate through repeated Bellman backups. The theoretical analysis shows how carefully restricting the actions selected during these backups can reduce this source of error.

The resulting practical algorithm is called bootstrapping error accumulation reduction, or BEAR. Across continuous control tasks, it learns robustly from multiple off-policy data distributions, including random experience and suboptimal demonstrations. These results support controlling the actions used in value updates as a way to improve learning from a fixed dataset. The contribution links a specific mechanism of instability to an algorithm designed to mitigate it.
neurips-2019-stabilizing-off-policy-q-le.tldr: BEAR stabilizes learning from fixed off-policy data by constraining backup actions to reduce accumulated bootstrapping error.

paragraphs: Many convex optimization problems can be expressed as semidefinite programs, combining a positive-semidefinite constraint with affine constraints. Classical solvers commonly assume that problem data are directly available. Machine learning and engineering applications often include stochasticity, creating a need for methods that can operate with uncertain or sampled information.

Frank-Wolfe-type methods offer a scalable approach by using a linear minimization oracle instead of projecting onto the semidefinite cone. This paper introduces a conditional-gradient method for stochastic optimization with affine constraints. Its contribution extends this style of optimization to a setting where both random information and explicit constraints must be handled.

The authors prove an expected objective residual rate of O(k^(-1/3)) and a feasibility gap rate of O(k^(-5/12)), where k counts iterations. The objective residual tracks progress toward the optimal objective value, while the feasibility gap tracks constraint violation. Reporting both matters because a useful constrained solution must make progress on the objective and satisfy the constraints. The guarantees quantify how the method improves on these two requirements as computation proceeds.
neurips-2019-stochastic-frank-wolfe-for-.tldr: A stochastic Frank-Wolfe-type method handles affine constraints with convergence guarantees for objective error and constraint violation.

paragraphs: Language understanding and generation involve different ways of using context. UniLM brings these capabilities into a shared pretrained model that can be fine-tuned for either kind of task. Its pretraining combines unidirectional prediction, bidirectional prediction, and sequence-to-sequence prediction within one Transformer network.

The mechanism is to change self-attention masks, which control what context a prediction can access. Different masks let the shared network operate under the context restrictions required by the three training tasks. This provides a concrete way to combine multiple language modeling behaviors while retaining a common set of network parameters.

UniLM compares favorably with BERT on GLUE and the SQuAD 2.0 and CoQA question answering tasks. It also reports state-of-the-art results on five generation datasets spanning summarization, question answering, question generation, and document-grounded dialogue. For example, CNN/DailyMail summarization reaches 40.51 ROUGE-L, an absolute improvement of 2.04, and SQuAD question generation reaches 22.12 BLEU-4, improving by 3.75. These results show that the unified pretraining approach supports both understanding and varied forms of text generation.
neurips-2019-unified-language-model-pre-.tldr: UniLM uses attention masks to train one Transformer for multiple language modeling tasks, supporting both understanding and generation.
